name: Lyttelton
title: Lyttelton Hull Gauging | UTM at the Dry Dock and Cashin Quay
description: Ship thickness gauging in Lyttelton for coal carriers, container ships, fishing vessels and tankers: dry dock hull readings, holds, ballast tanks and decks.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging at Lyttelton, the Port of Christchurch
intro: Lyttelton, the port for Christchurch and the largest in the South Island, lies inside a sheltered volcanic harbour on Banks Peninsula. Coal from the West Coast, containers, fuel, logs and vehicles cross its wharves, and its heritage dry dock is still at work docking fishing vessels, tugs, barges and the occasional small tanker. Gauging happens both in the dock and alongside. Atlantis has nobody stationed in New Zealand, and the technicians fly from India for each assignment.

highlights.h: A dry dock in steady use
highlights.p: Lyttelton Port Company's graving dock, opened in the 1880s, docks mostly fishing vessels, along with tugs, barges and the occasional small tanker, and is booked well ahead. A docking there is the chance to gauge bottom, side shell and sea chests while the hull is clean and dry.

Coal from the West Coast mines is railed across the Southern Alps and loaded at the port's coal terminal for steel makers in Asia. Bulk carriers in this trade show the hold frame, bracket and tank-top wastage that wet coal produces, and suit hold gauging during their loading calls.

Christchurch is a gateway for Antarctic programmes, and research and supply ships use Lyttelton before and after the southern season. Ice-strengthened hulls take heavy wear at the bow and along the waterline, and a port call or docking here gives time to measure it.

port.h: A crater harbour on Banks Peninsula, and the port's wharves
p: Lyttelton Harbour, Whakaraupō, fills the flooded crater of an extinct volcano on the northern side of Banks Peninsula, its steep hills rising straight from the water and separating the port from Christchurch on the plains beyond. A road tunnel and a rail tunnel through the Port Hills link the two, and the rail line carries coal and containers to and from the wharves. Ships enter from Pegasus Bay through the harbour heads and follow a dredged channel up to the wharves on the northern shore, with compulsory pilotage for larger ships. The harbour is well sheltered from the prevailing winds, although easterly weather can raise a swell at the entrance, and the tidal range is moderate. The old town climbs the slopes directly above the wharves, so flat port land is scarce and much of the new working space has had to come from reclamation.

Cashin Quay at the eastern end of the port holds the container terminal and the coal terminal, and the company has been reclaiming land at Te Awaparahi Bay to extend its container operations. Coal from the West Coast arrives by rail and leaves on bulk carriers, containers carry dairy, meat and other Canterbury produce out and consumer goods in, and imported vehicles, fertiliser, cement, logs and general cargo cross the inner wharves. Product tankers bring in fuel for Canterbury and much of the South Island through the port's oil berth. A dedicated cruise berth, opened in 2020, brought large cruise ships back to Lyttelton after years in which they had used Akaroa on the far side of the peninsula instead. Fishing vessels, tugs, coastal ships and research vessels share the inner harbour, and the dry dock sits beside the old town.

The Canterbury earthquakes of 2010 and 2011 damaged much of the port, and its wharves and land have been repaired, strengthened and extended in the years since, a programme that still affects which berths are in use at any time. Ship stays follow the cargo: container ships turn round in about a day, coal carriers stay while their stockpile is loaded, and tankers spend a day or two discharging. Cruise calls concentrate in the southern summer. Winter southerlies are cold but rarely stop work alongside inside the harbour, and the shelter of the crater means ships at the berths are seldom troubled by swell. Fishing vessels come into the dry dock for survey and maintenance between their fishing campaigns. Coal loadings depend on trains arriving from the West Coast, so a bulk carrier's time at the berth can stretch when rail deliveries are delayed.

facilities.h: The dry dock and the berths: where gauging happens at Lyttelton
p: Lyttelton is one of the few New Zealand ports where gauging can be done in dry dock as well as alongside. The port company's graving dock has served the harbour since the 1880s and docks around two dozen vessels in a typical year, most of them fishing vessels, along with tugs, barges and the occasional small tanker. Dockings run from about ten days to several weeks while contractors blast, paint and repair, and the dock is booked far in advance, so gauging is written into the owner's docking programme early. Readings are taken before blasting to assess the plating as found, with further points added on cleaned steel where the first results call for a closer look.

Alongside, bulk carriers at the coal terminal are boarded during their call, with holds gauged as the ship arrives empty and ballast tanks worked as the ballast plan allows. Container ships at Cashin Quay give a shorter window for deck, hatch coaming and tank readings, and tankers at the oil berth are gauged under the terminal's permit system. Car carriers, general cargo ships and fishing vessels at the inner wharves round out the work. Ships larger than the dock, which is most of the deep-sea fleet calling here, dry-dock in Asia, so their Lyttelton call is where measured steel data is gathered for the yard.

Cashin Quay container terminal — deck plating, coamings and tanks on container ships during their call

context.h: Inspection context at Lyttelton: Maritime New Zealand, the fishing fleet and the coal trade
p: Maritime New Zealand conducts port state control at Lyttelton under the Tokyo MoU and also regulates the New Zealand fishing fleet that uses the port, whose vessels must keep their maritime documents current under the country's survey regime. Fishing vessels work hard in the cold, rough waters off the east and south of the South Island, and a number of them are older ships bought second-hand from overseas, so wastage in the shell, fish holds, tanks and the engine-room sea water system is a constant concern. The Ministry for Primary Industries governs both fisheries and biosecurity, and vessels arriving from overseas, including those returning from foreign dockings or from Antarctic waters, must meet its biofouling and clearance requirements before working in New Zealand waters.

The coal trade is the other driver. Coal from the West Coast, much of it coking coal for steel making, is railed over the Southern Alps and stockpiled at the coal terminal before loading, and the bulk carriers that lift it sail for Asian mills and return in ballast or with other bulk cargo. Wet coal and its residues corrode hold frames, brackets and the lower parts of bulkheads, and coal dust works into hatch cover seals and drainage channels. Container ships and tankers calling at the port bring the familiar issues of deck and coaming fatigue and ballast tank coating breakdown. Because the deep-sea ships dock overseas, owners who use the Lyttelton call to gauge obtain readings that a distant yard can turn straight into a repair specification.

jobs.p: Lyttelton's jobs fall into two groups. Dockings of fishing vessels, tugs and small tankers in the port company's dry dock call for full hull gauging together with the internal tanks, holds and machinery space structure, planned with the owner and the dock's contractors so readings come before blasting and repair. Calls by bulk carriers, container ships and tankers that dock elsewhere call for owner's condition gauging, pre-docking estimates and pre-purchase inspections fitted around loading or discharge. Antarctic and research vessels occasionally add ice-belt and bow readings to that list. For every job the TM plan is drawn on the ship's own drawings before the team flies, and readings are delivered daily so repair and purchase decisions can be made while the ship is still in port.
list: Bottom, side shell and sea chest gauging on a deep-water trawler in the Lyttelton dry dock, together with fish hold and fuel tank readings.
Docking-survey gauging of a harbour tug or barge, with crack detection at towing fittings and fender supports.
Hold frame and tank-top gauging on a bulk carrier at the coal terminal before loading, with magnetic particle checks at bracket toes.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a container ship at Cashin Quay ahead of an Asian yard period.
Ice-belt and bow plating readings on a research or Antarctic supply vessel before or after its southern season.
Pre-purchase inspection of a fishing vessel or coastal tanker for a New Zealand buyer.

logistics: The team flies into Christchurch International Airport, usually connecting from India through an Australian or Asian hub or through Auckland, and reaches Lyttelton by road through the Port Hills tunnel. Indian nationals need a New Zealand visa that permits short-term specialist work, and we apply as soon as the docking date or port call is firm, with a supporting letter from the owner; processing times vary. Wharf access is arranged through the ship's agent, and dry dock work also follows the port company's site induction and permit system.

faqs.q: Can a fishing vessel be gauged in the Lyttelton dry dock?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is one of the most common jobs here. Bottom and side shell readings are taken from the dock floor and staging while the hull is clean, sea chests are measured with their gratings off, and fish holds, fuel tanks and the engine room are covered from inside. Because the dock is booked well ahead, we plan the gauging with the owner and the dock's contractors as soon as the docking date is known.

faqs.q: Can coal carrier holds be gauged during a loading call?
faqs.a: Before loading, yes. The ship arrives empty, and holds that are dry, ventilated and lit can be gauged from the tank top with access to the lower frames and brackets; upper frames and hatch coamings need staging or the ship's own access equipment. Once coal goes into a hold, work there stops, so we sequence the holds with the chief officer against the loading plan.

faqs.q: What if a ship is too large for the Lyttelton dry dock?
faqs.a: Most deep-sea ships calling here are, and they dock in Asia. For them, gauging alongside during the Lyttelton call gives the owner a measured steel list for the yard before the ship sails, instead of an allowance to be confirmed in dock. Readings are located on the ship's drawings so the yard can work from them directly when planning plate orders.

faqs.q: Can you inspect a ship coming back from Antarctic waters?
faqs.a: Yes. Ice-strengthened hulls take abrasion and impact damage along the ice belt and at the bow, and paint loss exposes the steel to fast corrosion. During a port call we gauge from inside the ballast and void spaces behind the ice belt; in dry dock the shell is measured from outside as well. Any biosecurity clearance the ship needs on its return is settled by the agent before shore staff board.
